c1.title: How a hand works
c1.body:
Texas Hold'em is played by two to ten people. Everyone gets two face-down cards that only they can see. Five community cards are dealt to the table step by step, and everyone uses them.

Before the deal, the two players to the dealer's left post forced bets: the small blind and the big blind. That way there is always something to play for. After each hand the dealer button moves one seat clockwise.

A hand goes through streets: preflop (just your two cards), flop (three community cards), turn (the fourth) and river (the fifth). Each street has a round of betting.

You win the pot in one of two ways: everyone else folds, or at showdown you have the best five-card hand.
c2.title: Hand rankings
c2.body:
The strength of a hand is its best five-card combination. Here they are from weakest to strongest.

High card — nothing made. Pair — two cards of the same rank. Two pair. Three of a kind — three cards of the same rank. Straight — five cards in a row, any suits; the ace can be high (10-J-Q-K-A) or low (A-2-3-4-5). Flush — five cards of one suit. Full house — three of a kind plus a pair. Four of a kind — four cards of the same rank. Straight flush — five cards in a row of one suit.

All suits are equal in poker. The rarer a hand, the stronger it is.
c3.title: Who wins
c3.body:
At showdown everyone makes their best five-card hand out of seven cards: their two and the five on the board. You can use both of your cards, one, or none.

If the hands are of the same type, compare ranks: a pair of kings beats a pair of queens. If the ranks are equal, the remaining cards decide — the kickers. Both have a pair of aces, but one has a king kicker and the other a queen: the king wins.

If the best five cards match in rank, the pot is split equally. This happens when the best hand is entirely on the board.
c4.title: Bets and actions
c4.body:
If nobody has bet on this street before you, you can check (pass) or bet.

If there is already a bet, you have three options: fold (throw your cards away), call (match the bet) or raise. The minimum raise is the same size as the last raise. Big blind 20, an opponent raised to 60, that is by 40 — you can raise to at least 100.

All-in means betting all your chips. If a bet is bigger than your stack, you can call all-in. Then you only play for the part of the pot you matched, and the rest goes to a side pot.

The betting round ends when everyone has matched the last bet or folded.
c5.title: Position and starting hands
c5.body:
Position is your seat relative to the dealer. The later you act, the more you know about your opponents. The dealer (button) acts last on the flop, turn and river — the best position. Seats right after the blinds are the hardest.

The main preflop rule: from early position play only strong hands, from late position play wider. Strong hands: big pairs (AA, KK, QQ, JJ), an ace with a high card (AK, AQ), suited high cards. Weak ones: unsuited, unconnected cards like 9-3 or 7-2.

When you enter a hand, raise more often than you just call the blind. A raise gives you a chance to take the pot right away.
c6.title: Outs and odds
c6.body:
An out is a card that improves your hand to one that will most likely win. Four cards to a flush: 13 − 4 = 9 cards of that suit are left in the deck, so you have 9 outs. An open-ended straight draw (for example 7-8-9-10) has 8 outs: any of the four sixes and four jacks. A gutshot (a gap inside, like 7-8-10-J) has 4 outs.

The rule of 2 and 4. On the flop multiply your outs by 4 to get your rough chance of making the hand by the river. On the turn multiply by 2 — that's the chance on one card. 9 outs on the flop ≈ 36%, on the turn ≈ 18%.
c7.title: Pot odds
c7.body:
Pot odds tell you whether a call is justified. The chance of winning you need = call ÷ (pot + call), where the pot already includes the opponent's bet.

Example: the pot is 100, an opponent bets 50. Now the pot is 150, the call costs 50, the total is 200. You need to win 50 ÷ 200 = 25% of the time. If your chance is higher, the call is profitable in the long run, even if you lose this time.

Compare with the rule of 2 and 4. With a flush draw on the turn (≈18%), calling a half-pot bet (needs 25%) loses money, while calling a quarter-pot bet (needs ≈17%) is close to break-even.
c8.title: Value bets and bluffs
c8.body:
A bet does one of two things: it takes chips from worse hands (a value bet) or makes better hands fold (a bluff).

With a strong hand, bet yourself: passive play leaves chips with your opponents. A sensible size is half to three quarters of the pot.

With a medium hand, such as a middle pair, checking is often better: a bet scares off worse hands and only better hands pay.

With a weak hand that almost never wins at showdown, bluffing is sometimes right — especially against one opponent who has shown weakness by checking. Bluff rarely: if you get called too often, bluffs lose chips.
c9.title: Reading opponents
c9.body:
Stats tell you who you're up against. VPIP is how often a player voluntarily puts chips in before the flop. PFR is how often they raise before the flop.

Tight-aggressive (VPIP 15–22%, PFR close to VPIP) plays few hands and plays them actively. Respect their bets.
Loose-passive (VPIP 40%+, low PFR) plays almost everything and mostly calls. Bluff them less, and bet more with strong hands — they will pay.
Loose-aggressive (VPIP 35%+, PFR 25%+) raises a lot. Call them more often with good hands.
Tight-passive (low VPIP and PFR): if they suddenly raise, they almost always have a strong hand.
c10.title: A winning strategy
c10.body:
Put it all together. Play fewer hands, but play them aggressively: pick strong starting hands, especially from early position, and enter with a raise. In late position play wider and bet when opponents show weakness.

Count the odds: a call is justified only if your chance of winning is higher than the price of the call. Bet for value with strong hands, bluff rarely and deliberately. Watch your opponents' stats and adapt.

And discipline. Keep a bankroll of at least 20 buy-ins for your stakes, and take a break after a losing streak: emotional decisions (tilt) cost the most.
